children: Japan Activation Capital is pushing its Japanese investee companies to take more risks and pursue growth opportunities that can otherwise be overlooked due to management's cautious approach.

The firm, founded in October 2023 by former Carlyle Group partner Hiroyuki Otsuka, has so far invested in seven Tokyo-listed companies. Armed with about $1.5 billion of investor commitments, it looks to add a couple more this year, said Otsuka, its chief executive.

JAC uses a private-equity firm's value-adding approach for listed companies, according to Otsuka. The firm works with management teams of its investee companies, acting as an insider to help them streamline operations and accelerate growth strategies, including overseas acquisitions, he said.

"We do it together. It's not our style to give instructions and push things forward," Otsuka said in an interview. He cited the reorganization of baby-care brand Pigeon's overseas businesses as an example of his firm's involvement.

After acquiring a stake in Pigeon in 2025, the firm helped the Tokyo-based company integrate Lansinoh Laboratories, its Alexandria, Va.-based unit, more closely with the rest of the group, Otsuka said. Pigeon acquired Lansinoh more than two decades ago and had allowed it to operate under independent management, he said.

JAC has invested across sectors, from consumer goods to industrial and electronics equipment. Its investees include dairy-food and confectionery maker Meiji Holdings, precision-instrument manufacturer Shimadzu and Omron, an electronics company known for industrial automation and medical equipment.

For at least six of its seven investments, JAC ranks among the top 10 shareholders, regulatory filings showed. In crane maker Tadano, it holds an 11% stake valued at about $120 million, making it the largest shareholder, and has a director on the board.

JAC typically holds a stake of between 2% and 10% and invests for three to four years. The firm avoids companies that operate only in Japan or industries with low valuations globally, Otsuka said. He added that Japanese companies often have low valuations due to prospects of slower growth, and that JAC is trying to change that perception.
The firm in June said it had expanded commitments from investors to 235 billion yen, equivalent to $1.47 billion.
Unlike activist investors, JAC invests only after management agrees to team up, Otsuka said, adding that the firm works with managements that have no intention of taking their companies private.
Otsuka said the firm can help companies carry out tasks together even when management is unsure of the outcome.

"You can't prove that a business is going to be 100% successful," he said. "Once you can demonstrate that you have a 40% to 50% [chance of success], all you have to do is to prove that by executing it."
